clue.text: As a working rule, gingerbread is served with raw cabbage

parts.note: parkin is a sticky oat-and-treacle gingerbread from northern England
is shortened to 's, giving S
food that is served is on, as in on the menu
slaw is shredded raw cabbage salad, as in coleslaw

explanation.surface: A cook's rule of thumb: gingerbread always comes with a side of raw cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: PARKIN is a Yorkshire gingerbread; IS contracts to S and SERVED gives ON, so PARKIN'S ON SLAW reads straight through.
explanation.definitionFit: This law is the jocular principle that work expands to fill the time available, a rule about how working goes.

clue.text: Celebrate the launch

explanation.surface: Toasting a new vessel as it goes down the slipway.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to spend lavishly on a celebration, and literally describes shoving a vessel off into the water.

clue.text: Coward lost head — "Nevermore!" he said

indicators.note: losing its head means the word for coward drops its first letter

parts.note: a craven is a coward

explanation.surface: A coward loses his nerve and cries that he will never do it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward' looks like Noel Coward; it is just a coward, CRAVEN. The definition alludes to Poe's poem, where the bird's only word is 'Nevermore'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Edgar Allan Poe's poem the black bird answers every question with the single word 'Nevermore'.

clue.text: Half-hearted lies — true or false?

indicators.note: false suggests the words are not genuine, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone unsure whether the lies they are told are true or not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false' rearranges the letters of LIES TRUE OR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone half-hearted lacks determination, wavering and undecided.

clue.text: Make firm road if land flooded underneath

indicators.note: in a down clue the marshland comes underneath, at the bottom of the entry

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a road
taken as written
a fen is low marshy land often under water, as in East Anglia's Fens

explanation.surface: Advice to harden a road in case the land below it floods.
explanation.definitionFit: To stiffen something is to harden or make it rigid.

clue.text: Not a positive difficulty

explanation.surface: A difficulty that is described as anything but a plus.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as NON PLUS it reads 'not a positive'; as a noun, nonplus is a state of perplexity.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally non (not) plus (a positive); as a noun it means a quandary or perplexity.

clue.text: Hair fastener

explanation.surface: A clip for holding hair in place.
explanation.definitionFit: A lock is a tress of hair, and also a device that fastens a door.

clue.text: Roundabout where old politician embraces one flighty girl

indicators.note: embraces means the old politician's name holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: the Whigs were the historical British party opposed to the Tories
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: flighty, fickle and restless, tells us to rearrange the letters of girl

explanation.surface: A fairground ride where an old statesman hugs a giddy young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flighty' rearranges GIRL; that and I sit inside the old party name, splitting it after its second letter. 'Roundabout' is the fairground ride, not the traffic junction.
explanation.definitionFit: A whirligig is a merry-go-round or anything that spins round and round.

clue.text: Tudor Minister of Transport — certainly depression rises around one

parts.note: a car is a means of transport

indicators.note: around means the reversed run is wrapped around the letter for one
in a down clue rising means the words for certainly and depression are read upwards together, so backwards

parts.note: yes means certainly
lowland is low-lying ground, a depression in the landscape
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A Tudor-era transport secretary watching hollows rise around him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' looks like part of a ministry title but just gives CAR. 'rises' reads YES and LOWLAND upwards as one run (DNALWOLSEY), and 'around' wraps that round I, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Wolsey was Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor and chief adviser, the dominant Tudor statesman of his day.

clue.text: Grieves on changing money

indicators.note: changing tells us to alter the order of these letters

explanation.surface: Someone mourns as they change their cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges GRIEVES ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign is an old British gold coin worth one pound.

clue.text: Tea passed round in this?

indicators.note: passed round means the word for tea goes around the other word

parts.note: cha (or char) is British slang for tea
taken as written

explanation.surface: Teacups being handed round at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read as wordplay it builds the answer, and read plainly it asks what tea is handed round in.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine porcelain cups and saucers are what tea is poured into and handed round.

clue.text: Societies with uplifting effect

explanation.surface: Clubs that raise people's spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Tongs are Chinese secret societies; the second reading is a playful description of a tool that lifts things.
explanation.definitionFit: A tong is a Chinese secret society; the tool of the same name grips and lifts coal or food.

clue.text: Dropped stitch

explanation.surface: A knitter's lost stitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Fell is the past tense of fall, so dropped; a fell is also a seam stitched flat.

clue.text: Vehicle, second to start with, went ahead later

indicators.note: to start with means only the opening letter of second is used

parts.note: led means went ahead, at the front

explanation.surface: A vehicle that came second at the start and took the lead later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'later' just places LED after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A sled is a sledge, a vehicle on runners for snow.

clue.text: Flat broke

explanation.surface: Living in a flat and out of money.
explanation.definitionFit: Down and out describes a boxer floored and counted out, and also someone destitute with no money.

clue.text: One slip, and the letter's rewritten

definitions.note: the letter's stands for the letter is

indicators.note: rewritten means these letters are written again in a different order

explanation.surface: A single slip, and the letter has to be written again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewritten' rearranges ONE SLIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Twirl a lot of snowdrops into a spray

parts.note: to twirl is to spin
snow that drops in quantity piles up into a drift

explanation.surface: Spinning a bunch of snowdrop flowers into a bouquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snowdrops' looks like the flowers, but here it is snow dropping, and a lot of it is a DRIFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Spindrift is fine spray blown off the crests of waves, or windblown snow.

clue.text: Nought's wrong with such a wedding

indicators.note: wrong means the letters are set out incorrectly and need reordering

parts.note: the word nought with its s

explanation.surface: Nothing goes wrong at a wedding like this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges NOUGHTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A forced marriage arranged in haste because of a pregnancy is said to be at the point of a gun.

clue.text: Not included in dictionary, slang word for hand

indicators.note: in means the slang word goes inside the dictionary's abbreviation

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
mitt is slang for a hand

explanation.surface: A slang term for a hand that the dictionary leaves out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something omitted has been left out.

clue.text: See nothing dry up and wither on the outside

indicators.note: on the outside means the word for wither encloses the rest

parts.note: to die is to wither away
O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading the word for dry backwards

parts.note: sec means dry, of wine

explanation.surface: Watch nothing dry up and shrivel at the edges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb but is a bishop's see. 'up' reverses the word for dry, as befits a down clue; 'on the outside' wraps it with nothing in the word for wither.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop's see is the district under that bishop's authority.

clue.text: Country roads go the wrong way, say, in the interior

indicators.note: in the interior means the example abbreviation sits inside the roads
going the wrong way means the word for roads is read backwards

parts.note: lanes are narrow roads
eg (for example) means say

explanation.surface: In the heart of the countryside, the roads seem to run the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go the wrong way' reverses the roads, and 'in the interior' sets the abbreviation for say in their middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Senegal is a West African nation.

clue.text: African — his law I broke

indicators.note: broke means the words are broken up and their letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A confession from an African: I broke his law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' rearranges HIS LAW I.
explanation.definitionFit: Swahili is a Bantu language widely spoken in East Africa, so the word names something African.

clue.text: Arrange backing for a season

indicators.note: backing means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: to edit is to arrange text

explanation.surface: Planning support for a time of year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns EDIT round. Tide is old for a season, as in Eastertide.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage a tide is a time of year, surviving in Yuletide and Whitsuntide.

clue.text: In wartime no more game ducks

parts.note: nap is a card game
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, O, so two ducks give OO

explanation.surface: During the war, game birds like ducks were off the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: NAPOO was First World War soldiers' slang for finished or gone, from French il n'y en a plus.
explanation.definitionFit: The First World War slang term meant finished, gone or dead.

clue.text: Drop round

explanation.surface: A rounded droplet.
explanation.definitionFit: To plump down is to drop heavily, and plump also means chubby or rounded.

clue.text: Pure water

explanation.surface: Clean, fresh water.
explanation.definitionFit: Mere means nothing more than, sheer; a mere is also a lake.

clue.text: One in two records strangely, use last addresses

indicators.note: in means the letter for one sits between the two records

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
a log is a record, as in a ship's log
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: strangely means the following word's letters appear in an odd order

explanation.surface: A single track on a double album, played oddly as a farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in two records' puts I between the two record words; 'strangely' rearranges USE, which goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Epilogues are closing speeches delivered to the audience at the end of a play.

clue.text: They held back a vessel, and experienced serious consequences

indicators.note: held means the word they grips the rest inside it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back means the vessel and the experience are read in reverse

parts.note: a pot is a vessel
lived means experienced

explanation.surface: Sailors who kept a ship back faced grim repercussions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses A POT and LIVED as one run, giving DEVILTOPA; 'held' sets that inside THEY. 'vessel' suggests a ship, but it is only a pot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes trouble to be faced, punishment or a heavy reckoning ahead.
